Effects of grain boundaries on the evolution of radiation-induced bubbles in polycrystalline tungsten: A phase-field simulation

Abstract

Tungsten (W) is widely recognized as a promising material for plasma-facing components in nuclear fusion reactors, and the evolution of bubbles in polycrystalline tungsten significantly impacts its properties. This study developed a phase-field model considering elastic inhomogeneity to investigate the evolution of radiation-induced bubbles. The Gibbs free energy of helium bubbles was derived using the Van der Waals equation. An explicit nucleation algorithm accounting for the position of grain boundaries (GBs) was coupled to the model. Furthermore, the model also considered the inequality between the internal pressure of the bubble and the surface tension. The growth kinetics of a single bubble with elastic heterogeneity were examined, and based on these findings, the evolution of bubbles under irradiation was simulated, yielding results consistent with experimental observations. Furthermore, the influence of GBs on radiation-induced bubbles was investigated using the developed model. The simulation results demonstrated that both GBs, as preferential nucleation regions and as sinks for vacancy absorption, had an impact on bubble nucleation and growth. The superior radiation resistance observed in nanocrystalline tungsten was dominantly attributed to the absorption of vacancies by GBs.

1. Introduction

Due to its high melting point, high thermal conductivity and sputtering resistance, tungsten is a promising plasma-facing material for nuclear fusion reactors [1,2]. Plasma-facing materials will experience a high flux of neutral and He ions, and these particles bombard the tungsten surface, resulting in radiational damage and He implantation [3,4]. Under such high irradiation levels, gaseous species such as He generated by irradiation tend to accumulate to form gas bubbles because of their low solubilities in tungsten [5]. These existing He gas bubbles will grow through absorbing supersaturated radiation-induced vacancies and gas atoms [6]. The distribution and kinetic of bubbles have an essential effect on the deterioration of material properties such as swelling and reduced thermal conductivity [7,8]. Therefore, it's critical for predicting the long-term behavior of nuclear materials to research and understand the evolution of bubbles during irradiation.
Nanocrystalline tungsten was reported as a highly radiation-resistant material due to its high grain boundary (GB) density and small bubble size [9]. However, bubble evolution in polycrystal nuclear materials is a complex multi-physics process, including many competing and interacting mechanisms that are affected by existing structural characteristics such as GBs and dislocations. In order to figure out the influence of GB on bubble evolution during irradiation, a series of experimental researches were carried out in polycrystalline tungsten [9], [10], [11], [12], [13], [14], [15]. On the one hand, GBs as priority areas for bubble nucleation lead to a larger bubble. On the other hand, the GB as a sink can absorb point defects that will inhibit the bubble format and growth. As El-Atwani et al. concluded [9], ultrafine grain tungsten has excellent performance in radiation resistance. Due to the large GB area in nano-grain tungsten, the size and density of the bubble remain low during irradiation. Therefore, to quantitatively calculate the bubble evolution in polycrystalline tungsten, it is necessary to understand the influence of GB on bubble evolution.
In the past several decades, different scale modeling methods have been applied to study the behavior of radiation-induced bubbles in tungsten, including ab initio calculation (DFT) using density functional theory [16,17], classical molecular dynamics (MD) [18,19] and kinetic Monte Carlo method (KMC) [20,21]. Each of these methods has limitations since the usability for a specific time and scale range. With the requirements of considering thermodynamics and dynamics simultaneously in the mesoscopic scale, the phase-field method (PFM) has unique advantages because its driving force is the reduction of free energy in the simulation of microstructure evolution. In the past several decades, PFM has been successfully applied to the research of grain growth [22,23], void and bubble evolution [24], [25], [26], [27], and the interaction between GB and pore [28], [29], [30] in nuclear material. In addition, PFM can well couple the microelastic theory considering the stress and strain provided by microstructure. Wang et al. [31] established a phase-field model of void evolution based on the elastic strain energy, which was used to study the effects of neutron irradiation and elastic tensile load on the microstructure evolution of polycrystalline tungsten. However, there is still a lack of a phase-field model of bubble evolution coupling elastic strain energy and considering the influence of GB simultaneously, which is essential to simulate and predict the bubble evolution in polycrystalline tungsten.
In this work, a phase-field model considering elastic heterogeneity of radiation-induced bubble evolution in polycrystalline tungsten is proposed based on the Kim-Kim-Suzuki (KKS) formulation. Based on the van der Waals equation, the Gibbs free energy of He bubble was derived, and the internal pressure of bubble was also introduced into the present model. An explicit nucleation theory of bubbles related to the position of GBs was also coupled to the model. The current model was applied to simulate the evolution of a single bubble. The effect of elastic energy on the single bubble growth is discussed by considering the elastic potential generated by a single bubble. The bubble evolution process under irradiation is simulated by introducing the source terms. The radius and density of bubble obtained under different DPAs are consistent with the experimental measurement. Moreover, with the introduction of polycrystal tungsten structure, the effects of enhanced bubble nucleation on the evolution of bubbles are studied. Furthermore, the impact of the absorption of vacancies by GBs on the evolution of bubbles has also been studied. Considering these two effects comprehensively, the grain size effects on the evolution of bubbles were quantitatively discussed. It is clarified that the ultrafine grain tungsten with a large GB area will inhibit bubble format and growth, which will strengthen the radiation resistance of tungsten.

2. Phase-field model

Considering the evolution of helium bubble and grain growth, a mesoscale phase-field model combining an iterative method for numerically solving the elastic equilibrium equation is presented in this section. To simulate the evolution of He bubble in polycrystalline tungsten, a pair of conserved field variables are used in this phase field model: a vacancy concentration cv (r, t) and a gas atom concentration cg (r, t). These phase field variables consider the radiation-induced vacancies and He gas atoms that can agglomerate into clusters or be absorbed by existing bubbles by diffusing freely in the domain. The analyzed microstructure in tungsten is divided into two distinct and stable phases: a matrix phase and a bubble phase. Typically, the initial point defects concentration in the matrix phase is supposed to be thermodynamic equilibrium concentration with cv = cveq, cg = cgeq. Bubbles are formed by the accumulation of vacancies and He gas atoms for simplifying. Thus, the bubble phase is assumed to be filled with vacancies and gas atoms with cv + cg = 1.0. To differentiate these two phases in space, a non-conserved order parameter η (r, t) takes a value of η = 0.0 in the matrix phase while η = 1.0 in the bubble phase. In addition, a set of non-conserved order parameters ϕi represent the different orientations of grains, whose value is equal to one within the corresponding grain while equal to zero within the others, similar to Chen's work [32]. All the phase field variables are continuous and vary smoothly across the diffuse interface.

2.1. Total free energy

In the present phase field model, a total free energy function of the heterogeneous system is built as a combination of chemical free energy, a double-well potential, gradient energy, polycrystalline energy, and elastic strain energy. Following the definition of free energy proposed by Aagesen [33], the total free energy F of the system is described as(1)𝐹=∫𝑉[𝑓𝑐⁢ℎ⁡𝑒⁢𝑚+𝑊⁢𝑔⁡(𝜂)+𝜅𝜂2⁢|𝛻𝜂|2+𝑞∑𝑖=1𝜅𝜙2⁢|𝛻𝜙𝑖|2+𝑓𝑝⁢𝑜⁢𝑙⁢𝑦+𝑓𝑒⁢𝑙⁢𝑎⁢𝑠]𝑑𝑉where fchem is the chemical free energy density, g(η) = η2(1-η)2 represents a double-well potential. At the same time, W is the height of the potential, κη and κϕ are the gradient energy coefficient, fpoly is the polycrystalline energy density, and felas is the elastic strain energy density, respectively.
The chemical free energy density that consists of the free energy density of matrix and bubble phases is written as(2)𝑓𝑐⁢ℎ⁡𝑒⁢𝑚=[1−ℎ⁡(𝜂)]⁢𝑓𝑚⁡(𝑐𝑚𝑣,𝑐𝑚𝑔)+ℎ⁡(𝜂)⁢𝑓𝑏⁡(𝑐𝑏𝑣,𝑐𝑏𝑔)where f m and f b are the chemical free energy density of the matrix phase and the bubble phase; cvm and cgm are the concentrations of vacancy and gas atom in the matrix phase; cvb and cgb are the concentrations of vacancy and gas atom in the bubble phase, respectively h(η) is an interpolating function with the form of h(η)=η3(6η2–15η+10) ensures the free energy density transitions smoothly between the matrix phase to bubble phase from h(0)=0 to h(1)=1.
The formulation of free energy density in the matrix phase is derived from thermodynamics consisting of the entropic and enthalpy of point defects, which is written as(3)𝑓𝑚=𝐸𝑓𝑣⁢𝑐𝑚𝑣+𝐸𝑓𝑔⁢𝑐𝑚𝑔+𝑘𝐵⁢𝑇⁢[𝑐𝑚𝑣⁢ln⁡(𝑐𝑚𝑣)+𝑐𝑚𝑔⁢ln⁡(𝑐𝑚𝑔)+(1−𝑐𝑚𝑣−𝑐𝑚𝑔)⁢ln⁡(1−𝑐𝑚𝑣−𝑐𝑚𝑔)]where Evf and Egf are the formation energies of vacancy and gas atoms, kB is Boltzmann's constant, and T is the absolute temperature with a unit of Kelvin.
The bubble phase is treated to be filled by vacancies and gas atoms. In the present work, considering the configuration of vacancies and gas atoms in a bubble, the free energy density in the bubble phase is described as(4)𝑓𝑏=𝑐𝑏𝑔⁢𝑘𝐵⁢𝑇⁢(1𝑉−𝑐𝑏𝑔⁢𝑏−1𝑉⁢(1+ln⁡(𝑛𝑄⁢(𝑉𝑐𝑏𝑔−𝑏))))+𝐴⁢(1−𝑐𝑏𝑣−𝑐𝑏𝑔)2where the first term is the Gibbs free energy density derived from the van der Waals equation of helium reference to thermal physics [34]. V is the volume of the He gas atom, nQ is the quantum concentration, and b is the van der Waals constant. The second term is a parabolic function related to the concentration of vacancy and gas atom ensuring that cv + cg = 1.0 is kept in the bubble phase, and the value of the factor A = 6.4 × 1011 J/m3 was chosen [33]. Fig. 1 illustrates the bulk free energy function used in the present model.
In the present work, the evolution of grains with different orientations is coupled by a set of order parameters ϕi. Besides, the interaction of GBs and bubbles is considered in the present model by the polycrystalline energy density that is written as [28](5)𝑓𝑝⁢𝑜⁢𝑙⁢𝑦⁡(𝜂,𝜙𝑖)=𝜇⁢[∑𝑖(𝜙4𝑖4−𝜙2𝑖2)+𝑎𝐺⁡𝐵⁢∑𝑖∑𝑗>𝑖𝜙2𝑖⁢𝜙2𝑗+𝑎𝑠⁢∑𝑖𝜙2𝑖⁢𝜂2]where μ is the polycrystal parameter. aGB is the diffuse interface parameter of GB, taking a value of 1.5 [35]. And as is the diffuse interface parameter of free surface with a relationship as = aGB γs/γGB that is defined by the surface energy γs and GB energy γGB. The first term of creating p energy wells at each ϕi =1.0, and the last two terms ensure the free energy in GB and bubble surface is higher than in grain interior.

2.2. Elastic energy density

An assumption of liner elasticity is applied while the plasticity has been temporarily ignored in the current model. The elastic strain energy density caused by misfit is written as(6)𝑓𝑒⁢𝑙⁢𝑎⁢𝑠=12⁢𝐶𝑖⁢𝑗⁢𝑘⁢𝑙⁡(𝐫)⁢𝜀𝑒⁢𝑙𝑖⁢𝑗⁡(𝐫)⁢𝜀𝑒⁢𝑙𝑘⁢𝑙⁡(𝐫)where Cijkl (r) is the positional elastic constant tensor related to the grain orientations and bubbles. 𝜀𝑒⁢𝑙𝑖⁢𝑗⁡(𝐫) is the total elastic strain of the system. The mechanical equilibrium equation is written as(7)𝛻𝑗𝜎𝑖⁢𝑗⁡(𝐫)=𝛻𝑗[𝐶𝑖⁢𝑗⁢𝑘⁢𝑙⁡(𝐫)⁢(̅𝜀𝑖⁢𝑗+𝛿⁢𝜀𝑖⁢𝑗⁡(𝐫)−𝜀0𝑖⁢𝑗⁡(𝐫))]=0where 𝜎𝑖⁢𝑗⁡(𝐫) is the stress tensor of the system, ̅𝜀𝑖⁢𝑗 is the homogeneous strain, 𝛿⁢𝜀𝑖⁢𝑗⁡(𝐫)is the inhomogeneous strain, and 𝜀0𝑖⁢𝑗⁡(𝐫) is the eigenstrain, respectively.
In polycrystalline tungsten, the elastic constant tensor Cijkl (r) is always inhomogeneous due to the dependence on the orientation of different grains. Considering the rotation of grains with a fixed coordinate system, the position-dependent elastic constant tensor is written as [36](8)𝐶𝑖⁢𝑗⁢𝑘⁢𝑙⁡(𝐫)=∑𝑝𝜙⁢(𝐫,𝑡)𝑝⁢𝑎𝑝𝑖⁢𝑎⁢𝑎𝑝𝑗⁢𝑏⁢𝑎𝑝𝑘⁢𝑐⁢𝑎𝑝𝑙⁢𝑑⁢𝐶𝑚𝑎⁢𝑏⁢𝑐⁢𝑑+𝜂⁡(𝐫,𝑡)⁢𝐶𝑏𝑖⁢𝑗⁢𝑘⁢𝑙where 𝑎𝑝𝑛⁢𝑚(n,m = 1,2) is the transformation matrix representing the rotation of the given coordinate system in the p-th grain to the reference coordinate system. ϕp is the corresponding order parameter, 𝐶𝑚𝑎⁢𝑏⁢𝑐⁢𝑑 is the elastic moduli tensor of the tungsten matrix and 𝐶𝑏𝑎⁢𝑏⁢𝑐⁢𝑑 is the elastic moduli tensor of the He bubble, respectively. The transformation matrix aij is written as(9)𝑎𝑖⁢𝑗=[cos⁡𝛼sin⁡𝛼−sin⁡𝛼cos⁡𝛼]where α is the Euler angle of the given grain in two dimensions space which was randomly selected in each grain, and 0 ≤ α ≤ 2π. The bulk modulus E0 =1.17 GPa can be estimated by the equation of state (EOS) of He gas phase [37]. Therefore, the elastic constants of the bubble phase are assumed to be 𝐶𝑏11=1.8E0, 𝐶𝑏12=0.6E0 and 𝐶𝑏44=0.6E0 following Hu's work [38]. 𝐶𝑏11, 𝐶𝑏12 and 𝐶𝑏44 are the elastic constants of the bubble phase simplified by Voigt notation. The effect of elastic inhomogeneity from the bubble and different grain orientations are coupled in the current model [39].
A lattice misfit can occur in the matrix due to the introduction of point defects. Supposing the variation of the stress-free lattice parameter concerning defect concentrations follows Vegard's law, the eigenstrain contributed from the defect inhomogeneity in the matrix phase is written as [40](10)𝜀0⁢𝑚𝑖⁢𝑗=[𝜀𝑣⁢0⁢(𝑐𝑣−𝑐𝑒⁢𝑞𝑣)⁢𝛿𝑖⁢𝑗+𝜀𝑔⁡0⁢(𝑐𝑔−𝑐𝑒⁢𝑞𝑔)⁢𝛿𝑖⁢𝑗]⁢𝑗⁡(𝜂)where εv0 = (1/a)da/dcv and εg0 = (1/a)da/dcg are the expansion coefficients of the lattice parameter caused by the introduction of vacancies and gas atoms. cveq and cgeq are the thermal equilibrium concentration of vacancy and gas atom, δij is the Kronecker-delta function and j(η)=1-h(η), respectively.
Based on Xiao's work [41], the eigenstrain in the bubble phase is defined as(11)𝜀0⁢𝑏𝑖⁢𝑗=(𝑃𝑔−2⁢𝛾𝑠/𝑅)𝐸0⁢𝛿𝑖⁢𝑗⁢ℎ⁡(𝜂)where Pg is the pressure inside the bubble and 2γs/R represents the inward pressure around the bubble. When Pg is greater than 2γs/R for a bubble of definite size, the eigenstrain in the bubble phase is positive, which means the bubble is in a state of overpressure. If the eigenstrain in the bubble phase equals zero, it represents that the bubble is in a state of equilibrium between internal and external pressures. Similarly, the bubble is in a state of under pressure if the eigenstrain is negative. The pressure inside the bubble that can be derived by the equation of state is written as(12)𝑃𝑔=𝑐𝑔⁢𝑘𝐵⁢𝑇𝑉−𝑐𝑔⁢𝑏
Consequently, the total eigenstrain is(13)𝜀0𝑖⁢𝑗⁡(𝐫)=[𝜀𝑣⁢0⁡(𝑐𝑣−𝑐𝑒⁢𝑞𝑣)⁢𝛿𝑖⁢𝑗+𝜀𝑔⁡0⁡(𝑐𝑔−𝑐𝑒⁢𝑞𝑔)⁢𝛿𝑖⁢𝑗]⁢𝑗⁡(𝜂)+(𝑃𝑔−2⁢𝛾𝑠/𝑅)𝐸0⁢𝛿𝑖⁢𝑗⁢ℎ⁡(𝜂)
The homogeneous strain that represents the macroscopic shape change of the system is written as [42](14)̅𝜀𝑖⁢𝑗=𝑆𝑖⁢𝑗⁢𝑘⁢𝑙⁢𝜎𝑎⁢𝑝⁢𝑝𝑘⁢𝑙+1𝑉⁢∫𝑉𝜀0𝑖⁢𝑗⁡(𝐫)⁢𝑑3⁢𝑟+1𝑉⁢∫𝑉𝛿⁢𝜀𝑖⁢𝑗⁡(𝐫)⁢𝑑3⁢𝑟where Sijik = Cijkl−1 is the inverse of the elastic modulus tensor and 𝜎𝑎⁢𝑝⁢𝑝𝑘⁢𝑙 is the applied stress. The first term of the formula above considers the applied stress on the homogeneous strain, and the last two terms are the mean of the eigenstrain and the heterogeneous strain.
Considering the i th component of displacement ui(r), the heterogeneous strain obtained by the relationship of strain and displacement is written as(15)𝛿⁢𝜀𝑖⁢𝑗⁡(𝐫)=12⁢(𝜕𝑢𝑖⁡(𝐫)𝜕𝑟𝑗+𝜕𝑢𝑗⁡(𝐫)𝜕𝑟𝑖)
To compute the local elastic field, the mechanical equilibrium equation mentioned above was solved through an iterative perturbation scheme in the present work [39].

2.3. KKS model description

KKS model [43] requires that vacancies and gas atoms are conserved, and the overall vacancy concentration and gas atom concentration are described in terms of the phase concentration as(16)𝑐𝑣=[1−ℎ⁡(𝜂)]⁢𝑐𝑚𝑣+ℎ⁡(𝜂)⁢𝑐𝑏𝑣(17)𝑐𝑔=[1−ℎ⁡(𝜂)]⁢𝑐𝑚𝑔+ℎ⁡(𝜂)⁢𝑐𝑏𝑔
Furthermore, the KKS model assumes that the chemical potentials of the components in the matrix phase and bubble phase are the same, which is shown in the formula below as(18)𝜇𝑣=𝑑⁢𝑓𝑚𝑑⁢𝑐𝑚𝑣=𝑑⁢𝑓𝑏𝑑⁢𝑐𝑏𝑣(19)𝜇𝑔=𝑑⁢𝑓𝑚𝑑⁢𝑐𝑚𝑔=𝑑⁢𝑓𝑏𝑑⁢𝑐𝑏𝑔where μv and μg are the chemical potentials of vacancy and gas atom. In each phase field calculation step, the Newton-Raphson method is used to solve the Eqs. (16-19) to obtain local concentrations of different phases.
In the KKS model, the interfacial parameters such as gradient energy coefficient κη and double-well potential height W are related to the material properties including the surface energy γsurf and the interface thickness 2λ, which is shown as [33](20)𝛾𝑠⁢𝑢⁢𝑟⁢𝑓=√𝜅𝜂⁢𝑊3⁢√2(21)2⁢𝜆=2.2⁢√2⁢√𝜅𝜂𝑊where the interface thickness 2λ was chosen to be 3 nm, ensuring the interface width is about six net grids for numerical stability. The value of κη and W can be determined by Eqs. (20-21) to be κη=2.75×10−8 J/m and W = 2.95×1010 J/m3 through the specified γsurf and 2λ. Similarly, the parameters of GB, such as the gradient coefficient κϕ and the polycrystal parameter μ, have similar relationships with the material properties, including the GB energy γGB and the GB thickness lGB, which is expressed as [35](22)𝛾𝐺⁡𝐵=√2⁢𝜇⁢𝜅𝜙3(23)𝑙𝐺⁡𝐵=√8⁢𝜅𝜙𝜇where the GB thickness lGB was chosen to be 3 nm as well, and the value of κϕ and μ can be determined by Eqs. (22-23) to be κϕ=2.01×10−8 J/m and μ=1.79×1010 J/m3.

2.4. Evolution equations

The temporal and spatial evolution of conserved field variables including vacancy and gas atom is described by Cahn-Hilliard equations, which is written as(24)𝜕𝑐𝑣𝜕𝑡=𝛻·𝑀𝑣𝛻𝜇𝑣+𝑃𝑣−𝑅𝑣⁢𝑖−𝑆𝑣(25)𝜕𝑐𝑔𝜕𝑡=𝛻·𝑀𝑔𝛻𝜇𝑔+𝑃𝑔where Mv and Mg are the mobility of vacancy and He atom expressed by their corresponding diffusion coefficient as Mv =Dvcv/kBT and Mg =Dgcg/kBT, respectively. Pv and Pg are the source terms determining the introduction of point defects during irradiation. The production rate of vacancy can be expressed as(26)𝑃𝑣⁡(𝐫,𝑡)={0if𝜂≥0.8or𝑅1>𝑃𝑅2⁢𝑉𝐺if𝜂<0.8and𝑅1≤𝑃where P is the probability of a cascade event occurring at each grid point and time step, R1 and R2 are random numbers taking the value of zero to one, and VG is the increase of vacancy concentration when a vacancy is introduced. Further, the criterion η < 0.8 ensures the source term is only effective in the matrix phase. The total vacancy production rate is described as 𝐾𝑣=̅̅̅̅̅̅𝑉𝐺⁢𝑃 with a unit of displacement per atom (DPA) per unit of time [44], where ̅̅̅̅̅̅𝑉𝐺 is the average increase in vacancy concentration. Since the phase field variables used in this model do not consider the interstitials, in order to supplement the influence of interstitial and vacancy recombination on vacancies, an additional term that composites the recombination has been added to the dynamic equation of vacancy evolution. Rvi=Krcvm, where Kr is the effective recombination coefficient of vacancies. The use of vacancy concentration in the matrix is to ensure that this term only applies on the matrix. The purpose of introducing the recombination term in this phase field model is to maintain the vacancy concentration cv0≈8 × 10−3 away from bubbles, referring to Aagesen's work [33]. Therefore, the expression for Kr is VGP/2cv0.
The production rate of gas atom is defined as(27)𝑃𝑔⁡(𝐫,𝑡)=Λ𝑁𝑎⁢(1−𝜂)2⁢K𝑔where Na is the number of lattice sites per million, Λ is a constant of the He-appm/DPA ratio introduced by Harrison et al. [45], and Kg is the He gas atom production rate with a unit of DPA per time, respectively.
The absorption term Sv representing the absorption of vacancy by GBs is written as(28)𝑆𝑣⁡(𝐫,𝑡)=𝑠𝑣⁢(𝑐𝑣−𝑐𝑒⁢𝑞𝑣)⁢(1−Φ)where sv is a constant defining the absorption strength, and Φ is a function related to the location of GBs with a form Φ=∑𝜙2𝑖. The value of Φ equal to one within a grain and less than one in GB. For all order parameters η and ϕi are governed by the Allen-Cahn equations that are written as(29)𝜕𝜂𝜕𝑡=−𝐿𝜂⁢𝛿⁢𝐹𝛿⁢𝜂(30)𝜕𝜙𝑖𝜕𝑡=−𝐿𝜙⁢𝛿⁢𝐹𝛿⁢𝜙𝑖where Lη and Lϕ are the mobility of the bubble surface and GB. All parameters of tungsten used in the present simulation are shown in Table 1. During numerical implementation, the evolution equations are non-dimensionalized with non-dimensional grid spacing (𝑥=𝑙/𝑙*), time step (𝜏=𝑡/𝑡*) and diffusivity (̃𝐷𝑣=𝐷𝑣⁢𝑡*/𝑙*2 and ̃𝐷𝑔=𝐷𝑔⁢𝑡*/𝑙*2), using the characteristic length scale l*=1 nm and time scale t*=1 × 10−6 s. Periodic boundary conditions are used in this simulation. Furthermore, a semi-implicit Fourier spectral method is used to solve the variable-mobility Cahn-Hilliard equations Eqs. (24) and (25) and the Allen-Cahn equations Eqs. (29) and (30) in the present work [46].

2.5. Nucleation method

In the current phase-field method, an approach that introduces discrete nuclei is applied to model bubble nucleation. This nucleation method is to randomly determine the location where nucleation should occur using the nucleation theory. Then, the discrete kernels are artificially introduced into the model. Considering the homogeneous nucleation rate under classical theory [47], the probability of nucleation forming at an atomic position within a characteristic nucleation time interval can be calculated as(32)𝐽hom⁡(𝑡)=𝑍⁢𝑁⁢𝛽⁢exp⁡(−Δ⁢𝐺*hom/𝑘𝐵⁢𝑇)⁢exp⁡(−𝜏0/𝑡)where Z is the factor of Zeldovich, N is the lattice site in unit volume, β is atomic impingement rate, Δ⁢𝐺*hom is the activation energy for forming stable nuclei considering the homogeneous nucleation, τ0 is the incubation time and t is the time, respectively. Refer to Simmons et al's work [47], a functional model of nucleation rate with composition based on Eq. (32) is written as(33)𝐽hom⁡(𝑡)=𝑘1⁢exp⁡(−𝑘2/Δ⁢𝑐𝑣)where k1=ZNβ. The activation energy can be expressed as Δ⁢𝐺*hom=𝜋⁢𝛾2𝑠⁢𝑢⁢𝑟⁢𝑓/Δ⁢𝐺𝑎=𝜋⁢𝛾2𝑠⁢𝑢⁢𝑟⁢𝑓/(𝑐⁢𝑜⁢𝑛⁢𝑠⁢𝑡⁢Δ⁢𝑐𝑣) in two dimensional. ∆Ga is the phase transition energy per unit area related to the local supersaturated concentration ∆cv. However, nucleation in solid is always heterogeneous due to the non-equilibrium defect characteristic such as GBs. These heterogeneities increase local free energy, which will be released if the bubble nucleus is generated in these areas, resulting in a decrease in the activation energy barrier. Bubbles at GBs will evolve to be lenticular shape due to the trend of minimizing interfacial energy. Following the derivation from Porter's publication [48], the activation energy barrier for bubble nucleation at GBs can be described as(34)Δ⁢𝐺*hetΔ⁢𝐺*hom=𝑆⁡(𝜃)=12⁢(2+cos⁡𝜃)⁢(1−cos⁡𝜃)2where S is the scale factor of the activation energy barrier between heterogeneous and homogeneous nucleation, and θ is the equilibrium dihedral angle of lenticular bubbles which is related to the energy of surface and GB with θ=2arccos(2γGB/γsurf). Similarly, the nucleation rate at GBs is shown as(35)𝐽het⁡(𝑡)=𝑘1⁢exp⁡[−𝑘2⁢𝑆⁡(𝜃)/Δ⁢𝑐𝑣]
In a discretized area, the overall nucleation probability is calculated by(36)𝑃⁡(𝑡)=1−exp⁡(−𝐽⁢Δ⁢𝑡)where J(r,t)=ΦJhom+(1-Φ)Jhet is the overall nucleation rate related to the position, and ∆t is the time interval for calculating the nucleation probability. In the simulation, nucleation steps are performed at each time step and the nucleation probability is calculated for each supersaturated region with spatial characteristic. After calculating the probability, the location of nucleation can be determined. It is worth noting that the nucleation probability is set to zero if the atomic nucleus already exists. In addition, a depletion region of the concentration field is required while introducing a bubble nucleus for concentration conservation.

3. Results and discussion

3.1. Bubble growth with elasticity

In this section, the growth of a single bubble with elasticity is discussed to verify our model and study the effect of elastic strain energy on bubble evolution. The simulation domain of the entire system is divided into 64×64 grid points, and a matrix containing vacancy and gas atoms is introduced. A single bubble with a radius of 2 nm is initially implanted at the center of the area. The growth of the gas bubble is dependent on the chemical potential difference between the matrix phase and the bubble phase which drives point defects to diffuse into the bubble. As per the bulk free energy equation, the supersaturation concentration of vacancy and gas atoms in the matrix is necessary for bubble growth. Thus, to observe bubble growth clearly, the defect concentration in the matrix is set to 0.01, which is significantly greater than the thermal equilibrium concentration, while the defect concentration of the bubble phase is initialized to its corresponding equilibrium concentration in the bubble phase.
The morphology of the bubble is shown in Fig. 2 (a-b). The bubble grows to approximately 3.7 nm after a non-dimensional time τ =2000 due to the influx of vacancies and gas atoms from the matrix. The circular shape of the bubble is maintained during the growth process, resulting from the minimization of interface energy. Additionally, Fig. 2 (c-d) shows the distribution of corresponding phase-field variables on the central line. It is apparent that the value of the variables remains constant in the bubble phase during evolution, and the area of the bubble phase increases while the diffusion interface remains identical [58].
For an evolving bubble, its eigenstrain is defined by the difference between its inner pressure and surface-tension forces size according to Eq. (11). Regardless of hydrostatic stress, a bubble is in equilibrium if its internal pressure is equal to its surface-tensor forces. When a pressure excess (or insufficient) arises in the bubble, stress gradients form in its vicinity. If the stress does not exceed the yield limit of the solid, the stress field around the non-equilibrium bubble can be determined by elasticity theory. For tiny bubbles, the imbalance will be relieved by vacancy flow. The distribution of stress components σxx, σyy, and σxy around the single bubble mentioned in Fig. 2(b) is shown in Fig. 3, which is obtained by solving the mechanical equilibrium equation using an iterative method. It is worth noting that the value of stress is considered positive if the solid is in compression. As shown in the figures, the stress components σxx and σyy within the bubble are positive. In contrast, those on the vertical and horizontal sides around the bubble are negative, which means the solid around the bubble is in tension. This is because the internal pressure of the bubble in our simulation is lower than the surface tension forces, meaning that the bubble pressure is insufficient. As discussed in the publication of Olander [59], the stress balance of the deficit pressure bubble must be maintained by a slight contraction of the surface, resulting in the solid near the interface being in a state of tension.
To discuss the effect of elastic strain energy on the evolution of a single bubble, Fig. 4 shows a comparison of the elastic potential and the local chemical potential at different times. The elastic potential obtained by deriving the elastic energy to η and the local chemical potential obtained by deriving η from all free energies except elastic energy is plotted. The local chemical potential is not zero except at the interface, where there is a composition gradient. A negative value of the local chemical potential indicates that the bubble can grow, which is determined by the supersaturated defect concentration around the bubble. In contrast, a positive elastic potential indicates that it will inhibit bubble growth, consistent with the behavior of deficit pressure bubbles. At the start of the simulation, the initial concentration of defects around the bubble is high, resulting in a local chemical potential much larger than the elastic potential. As the simulation time reaches τ = 2000, the local chemical potential decreases significantly due to the gradually exhausted defects around the bubble, as shown in Fig. 2(d). However, the decrease in elastic potential is not obvious because the eigenstrain of the bubble decreases very little with the increase in the bubble size.
To further analyze the effect of elastic strain energy on bubble growth, the bubble radius varying with time is plotted in Fig. 5 using black and red solid lines. At the initial stage, the bubble grows rapidly due to the supersaturated concentration of point defects near the diffusion interface. With the depletion of defect concentration, the growth of bubbles becomes slow. As shown in Fig. 2(d), there is a depleted zone of defects around the diffusion interface. Comparing the two curves, it is found that the elastic strain energy has little effect at the initial stage of bubble growth because the chemical potential provided by bulk free energy is much greater than that provided by elastic strain energy. However, in the later stage when the local chemical potential becomes less pronounced, the influence of elastic potential becomes more significant, leading to the inhibition of bubble growth. Therefore, it is essential to consider the elastic strain energy when accurately modeling the growth kinetics of non-equilibrium bubbles.

3.2. Bubble evolution under irradiation

In order to examine the swelling of material, it is crucial to understand the size and density of bubbles that form under varying irradiation doses. The simulation of bubble evolution in single-crystal tungsten under irradiation is conducted using the current phase-field model. A 2D domain with a 256×256 grid is divided into a periodic area and initialized with the thermal equilibrium concentration of point defects. The introduction of vacancy and gas atom into the system is carried out in space and time, utilizing the source terms discussed in Eq. (26) and Eq. (28), resulting in an increase in their local concentration. Over time, the uneven distribution of defects leads to the accumulation of vacancy and gas atoms, resulting in the nucleation of a few bubbles, which grow by absorbing adjacent point defects.
When a DPA rate of 10−3 dpa/s, which was used in the experiment of irradiated tungsten [60], is applied to the source term, the governing equations are solved to obtain the evolution of the entire system. The morphology of the resulting bubbles is shown in Fig. 6. As the irradiation dose increases, more point defects are generated in the domain, increasing the probability of local nucleation calculated in each time step. The evolution of bubbles can be divided into two stages: nucleation and growth. During the early stage of bubble evolution, as shown in Fig. 6 (a, b), bubble nucleation is dominant, with the number of bubbles increasing while the size remains the same. The formed bubbles will absorb the surrounding vacancies and gas atoms to grow resulting in a reduction of the nucleation probability. Therefore, in the later stage of bubble evolution, the growth of bubbles becomes dominant.
Fig. 7 displays the distribution of stress components, namely σxx, σyy and σxy, around the bubbles depicted in Fig. 6. Positive stresses are present within the bubbles, while negative stresses are present in the regions surrounding the bubbles. The stresses are approximately zero without hydrostatic stress in areas far from the bubbles. The stress magnitudes within the bubbles are different as illustrated in Fig. 7. According to Eq. (11), the eigenstrain of a bubble is a function of the bubble radius, which is calculated at each time step using the connected area method algorithm. The valid points η=1.0 are connected if their edges touch, and two adjoining points are considered part of the same object if they are both on and connected along the horizontal or vertical direction. Finally, the area of each bubble can be obtained by counting the number of these objects.
Fig. 8 presents the statistical average radius of bubbles obtained from the present simulation under different irradiation doses, indicated by a red dotted line. As shown in the figure, the average bubble size increases with increasing irradiation dose, and the growth rate exhibits a sudden increase near DPA=1.25. This suggests that at low DPA levels, excess point defects tend to gather and form new bubble nuclei. However, as the DPA increases, defects are more likely to be absorbed by the already-formed bubbles. Furthermore, the bubble radius extracted from experimental data is plotted for comparison [60]. The results from the phase-field simulation are in good agreement with the experimental data.
The number density of bubbles is another crucial parameter in bubble evolution, in addition to their size. Fig. 9 depicts the exponential variation of bubble number density with DPA and compares it with experimental data. The results obtained from the phase-field simulation agree well with the experimental data. In the simulation, before DPA=1.0, bubbles increase rapidly due to bubble nucleation induced by the accumulation of point defects. As the number of bubbles increases, the defects in the matrix get absorbed by existing bubbles, resulting in a decrease in the nucleation rate. Although not apparent on the exponential plot, the number of bubbles decreases in the later stages of the simulation. The growth of larger bubbles results in a larger depletion zone of point defects, which causes a contraction of the surrounding smaller bubbles.

3.3. Bubble evolution in polycrystalline tungsten

As a microstructural feature of nuclear material, GB has an essential influence on the evolution of bubbles. On the one hand, GBs were shown to be a preferential area of bubble formation with larger bubbles compared to that in the grain matrices, according to the experiment of helium implantation on tungsten at 1223 K [14]. On the other hand, the GB is considered a sink that will absorb vacancies, which reduces the probability of nucleation of radiation-induced bubbles. In this section, considering the influence of GBs, the verified phase-field model is used to research the effect of grain size on bubble evolution in polycrystalline tungsten.
In order to further understand the effect of the absorption of vacancy by GBs on irradiated bubbles, the present phase-field model considering the absorption term is used to simulate the evolution of bubbles in polycrystalline tungsten. In this section, 16 randomly generated grains are introduced in the domain, and the thermal equilibrium concentration of point defects is set as the initial condition. The irradiation condition is set as DPA=1.0. Different absorption efficiency is applied to simulate the irradiation-induced bubble evolution. It is worth noting that the absorption efficiency constants sv chosen in this simulation are 0 to 0.1, which can be understood as the fraction of the vacancy being annihilated at the GBs is 0 to 10 % according to Eq. (28) in each step. The connection between the absorption efficiency constant and the actual physical factor may require to be determined through more microscopic simulation methods.
The morphology of microstructure and the corresponding stress distribution with different vacancy absorption efficiency is shown in Fig. 10. As shown in Fig. 10(a) when the absorption constant sv is equal to 0, vacancies will not be absorbed by grain GBs. The probability of nucleation is higher at GBs than at grain interior according to Eq. (35). However, due to the absorption of vacancies by GBs, the concentration of vacancy at and around GBs decreases, resulting in a decrease in nucleation probability. Fig. 10 (d-f) shows the corresponding stress distribution, and different stresses are distributed in other grains related to their orientation. According to Tonks's work [61], the elastic deformation will accelerate grain growth, and the softest grain orientations with the highest elastic energy density grow at the expense of other orientations. To quantitatively study the effect of vacancy absorption from GBs on bubble evolution, the porosity under different absorption constants sv is shown in Fig. 11 where the fitting curve of porosity with absorption efficiency is also plotted in red as p = 10−2(1.50+1.84exp(-x/0.0027)). It can be observed that the porosity decreases with increasing absorption efficiency. However, the effect of absorption intensity is not linear, as the larger the absorption constant, the closer the vacancy concentration near the GB is to the equilibrium concentration.
As previously discussed, GBs can enhance bubble nucleation, which is detrimental to radiation resistance. However, GBs also serve as defect sinks, absorbing vacancies and enhancing irradiation resistance. Therefore, the excellent radiation resistance observed in nanocrystalline tungsten results from the competition between these factors. To further investigate the effect of grain size on irradiated bubbles, the verified phase-field model considering the absorption of vacancies by GBs is employed to simulate bubble evolution in polycrystalline tungsten. The microstructure morphology under different grain sizes is shown in Fig. 12, with corresponding grain sizes of 181.0 nm, 64 nm, and 32 nm in Fig. 12 (a-c). It can be observed from Fig. 12 (a-c) that the number of bubbles increases as the grain size decreases. This is because smaller grains have larger GB areas, providing more nucleation sites for bubble formation. However, as shown in Fig. 12 (d-f), if the absorption of vacancies by GBs is sufficiently strong, it can inhibit bubble formation in small-sized grains.
To quantitatively analyze the effects of absorption efficiency and grain size on bubble evolution, the changes in porosity with grain size for different defect absorption efficiencies are shown in Fig. 13. Without considering absorption at GBs, and the porosity decreases as the grain size increases due to enhanced bubble nucleation. However, when absorption is taken into account, the porosity increases with increasing grain size. Moreover, the porosity is lower with higher absorption efficiency, particularly when the grain size is small. The solid curves in Fig. 13 represent the fitting lines for the corresponding absorption efficiency constants, following the approach used in El-Atwani's work [9]. The fitting line is p = 10−2(2.03+2.89exp(-x/78.20)), p = 10−2(2.61–1.21exp(-x/170.34)) and p = 10−2(2.31–1.85exp(-x/100.08)) with the constants sv=0, sv=0.005 and sv=0.01. In summary, it can be deduced that the main reason for the observed high radiation resistance in nanocrystalline tungsten is the stronger influence of defect absorption by GBs on bubble evolution compared to the enhanced nucleation of bubbles by GBs.

4. Conclusions

A phase-field model of radiation-induced bubble evolution with elastic inhomogeneity was developed. The Gibbs free energy of He bubble was derived from the Van Del Waals equation. This model is coupled with an explicit nucleation algorithm related to GB position, which is applied to simulate the bubble evolution in polycrystalline tungsten, and the effect of GBs on bubble evolution was studied as well. The main conclusions from previous studies can be drawn as follows:
  • (1)
    The growth kinetics of a single bubble were investigated using a phase-field model, considering the influence of elastic energy. In the case of a non-equilibrium bubble, the presence of a pressure imbalance between the inside of the bubble and the surface tension resulted in the generation of additional free energy, which affected the evolution of the bubble. It was observed that under-pressure bubbles exhibited slower growth rates due to the requirement of additional gas atoms to compensate for the internal pressure of the bubble.
  • (2)
    The bubble evolution and the corresponding stress distribution under different irradiation conditions are simulated. The evolution of bubbles was divided into nucleation and growth stages, and the variation of bubble radius and density with displacement per atom (DPA) was determined by the combined influence of these two stages. Furthermore, the phase-field simulation results exhibited good agreement with experimental measurements.
  • (3)
    The influence of the GB as a priority region for bubble nucleation and as a sink absorbing vacancies on radiation-induced bubbles was investigated. As the absorption efficiency of vacancies at GBs increases, the probability of bubble nucleation decreases, resulting in a decrease in porosity. The strong absorption effect at GBs is deduced to explain the excellent radiation resistance in nanocrystalline tungsten.
